So I would like, if possible, for the Prosecution to elaborate on that so we could get a better feel for it. Specifically with respect to the notes, I would just urge the Court to look at Rule 68 and I think those notes were requested because Mr. Nikolic made them immediately upon his arrest and after his arrest. And I think given the information sheet that we did receive we would like to see what the basis of some of his defence was and what he may have relied on, we think it may lead to some exculpatory information. We don't know that, but I think because it is a document or documents that may provide some discoverable material that the Court should with all due respect order Mr. Nikolic to turn those documents over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But you agree that these documents are not at the disposal of the Prosecution, don't you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not requesting the Court to compel the Prosecution to turn them over; I'm asking the Court to enter an order like you have in the past with other witnesses which you have that power and discretion to do and order those witnesses to produce those relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, when they were testifying and making use of them here. Yes, but anyway, I'll refer the first part of your intervention to Mr. McCloskey for any remarks he may wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. -- we still speak to Mr. Nikolic, and if there's any -- if there's an order about the notes we'll help to facilitate them, and it hasn't -- communication has not broken down. I'm not saying that. The -- one of the statements that Mr. Nicholls took, as I recall it, Momir Nikolic made a statement about why he turned his -- changed his statement about the Kravica warehouse and he had an explanation for that which we did not find as credible. And that was something that was -- it was significant that we don't find as credible. That is one of the main points, but that in balance, we thought that overall his testimony would not be necessary for this -- for this prosecution, and that in balancing the probative value of his testimony, we didn't feel it was necessary. It's as simple as that. I mean, I can go into factual details about how I think we've proven his -- some of the information he would testify through other witnesses, but I don't think anyone wants to hear that. And I can, of course, explain in more detail if you're interested, but that's obviously the Prosecution's business as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have discussed on this. There's nothing that we need to say or we have to say about your decision to withdraw your witness, Mr. McCloskey. That's your decision. As for the Beara confidential motion, you have no objection that we deal with it in open session now at this stage or do you wish to go in private session, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour. I was just out of an abundance of caution because I wasn't sure if he was going to ask for a pseudonym or any protective measures. We filed it in that vein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this point, actually, we had come prepared already to dispose of this motion not knowing that this witness was being withdrawn by the Prosecution. We agree with you that it is not necessarily moot, because this witness can eventually be called either by yourselves or by us. So we are deciding the motion now orally. On the 28th of October, the Beara Defence team filed confidentially an expedited motion requesting the Trial Chamber to issue a subpoena duces tecum in relation to would be then witness Momir Nikolic, expedited because of the anticipated proximity of his testimony here. On the 31st of October the Prosecution filed a response confidentially upon our request to do so expeditiously. The Trial Chamber has gone through these two filings and accepts fully the arguments provided by the Prosecution in their response on the basis of which we consider the Beara motion to be without merit. The motion itself provides no basis in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence or the jurisprudence of this Tribunal for the relief sought. Accordingly, we are hereby dismissing the motion. Let's decide also another oral motion that was raised yesterday, but before we do so, since we're talking of the testimony of General Smith, and it may also be relevant to the testimony of the Canadian, Guy Fortin, Mr. Fortin, we had invited you, Mr. McCloskey, to sit together with Madam Fauveau and to try to conclude the issue relating to the -- her motion on behalf of her client, General Miletic for the complete disclosure to the Defence of all UNPROFOR documents relevant to the present case. I also asked you a couple of days ago whether there had been some development, and I got the impression that although there had been, searches were still ongoing. So if you could both update the Trial Chamber on that, please, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, and -- there are two subjects to that, and as Mr. Thayer, I think, has the most up to date and thorough knowledge on that, I would turn the floor over to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer. Don't worry. I'll watch you on the monitor. I can't see you behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone. We are in a position to update the Chamber on those issues. There are a couple of related issues to these witnesses in addition to the specific request enumerated in Madam Fauveau's motion. I'll start with that first. What we have been doing is conducting multiple database searches using key words and date ranges based on her requests. The requests are very, very broad, so it's taken some time to respond to them. In some respects they are almost too broad to respond to, but what we've done is done our best to isolate what we can. What that has resulted in is a batch of documents that we are in the process of reviewing and sending for Rule 70 clearance. Because the request pertains to UN documents, naturally the -- virtually all of them have fallen within UN -- various UN archives and are thus protected under Rule 70 by those various providers be it the ICFY, the International Commission for the former Yugoslavia or another Geneva-based archive or yet another UN-based entity. So what we have done is we have kicked out a corpus of documents which we believe are broadly responsive to that very broad request of Madam Fauveau. We are in the process of submitting those for Rule 70 clearance to the UN. I cannot provide really any useful estimate as to how long it's going to take the UN to clear these documents. The only thing I can tell the Court is based on my recent experience in trying to get the Fortin diary cleared and the 11 documents which I think you heard discussion of last week plus one other additional document, the process of having these documents cleared in the immediate future are pretty slim. However, we will do our best to bring whatever pressure we can to bear to get those cleared as soon as we can. That said, there is smaller group of documents which I just finished reviewing this morning which have already been cleared which we will be in a position to disclose to Defence counsel, I would say, by sometime this afternoon. Those again are, we believe, broadly responsive to the very broad request of Madam Fauveau, and we will get that burned onto CDs and placed in the lockers, hopefully, by the close of business today. I think that's as much as I can say with respect to -- to the motion. Again, the Fortin diary has been cleared for use by the UN with certain restrictions that I've alerted my friends to earlier in the week, that being that we keep the information contained in the diary in private session, we treat and maintain the confidentiality of that information, but in all other respects the diary can be used. We are in the process of finding out exactly what has happened with these 11 documents plus the one other document that was submitted some time ago. I will have an update later on today. I have been told that the most difficult level of clearance has been achieved for those documents and we are awaiting a subsequent level of clearance. That's about as much, I think, as I can tell Your Honours at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. As regards Madam Fauveau, if you wish to comment after having heard that, in particular I think the Fortin testimony comes later, and we still have some time left. But General Smith will be here soon. It's true that he will be testifying in two separate stages. So we would like to know what your position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, indeed, yesterday and the day before yesterday we received a number of documents related to General Smith. Having said that, the Prosecutor also told us that these documents are not relevant to my motion and that they would have been disclosed in any case without my motion. I do not believe that my motion is broad in nature, because the documents I'm requesting only refer to General Smith, and they are documents received by General Smith or drafted by General Smith. I may understand that the Prosecutor has problems where the -- General Smith was one of the addressees of the documents. I do not believe that my request for the documents produced by General Smith during the relevant period can come as a surprise to the Prosecutor, because even if these documents are not directly linked to Zepa and Srebrenica, they are linked to what took place in Bosnia. General Smith is partly an expert witness, and it is common practice for the Prosecutor to disclose all the documents produced by a witness and that the Prosecutor has at its disposal. I know that my motion came late, so I do not want General Smith's testimony to be delayed, but still I would like to keep the possibility of having an additional day for further cross-examination that might prove necessary on the basis of the documents that might be disclosed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. One question: Have these documents ever been used in any other proceedings before this Tribunal? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- the documents that I referred to being kicked out by our searches conducted specifically with respect to Madam Fauveau's request, as I understand it have never been used before. Had they been used before, we would have expected to have seen that they'd been cleared before. One part of our process during these searches has been to compare them against all of our known disclosure lists to see whether in fact that was the case, and none of these documents, with the exception of the smaller group that I referred to which we hope to disclose today, have been previously disclosed. I think that's about as much as I'll say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Broadly speaking, I support what my learned friend, Madam Fauveau has just said, Your Honour. Clearly if there are additional pertinent documents that are yet to be disclosed, then they are likely, as far as this area of the case is concerned, to impact upon General Smith. They're very unlikely, frankly, only to impact upon Mr. Fortin. If they relate to him, they're almost certainly bound to relate to General Smith as well. Secondly, and aside from that, I was actually discussing this with Mr. Thayer at the last break. He had explained very helpfully in an e-mail earlier this week the position so far as Mr. Fortin's diary is concerned. At this present moment, I wish to reserve our position as to whether we're going to argue whether that diary can and should only be used in private session. I'm only alerting the Court to that simply because he's mentioned it, and therefore I don't want it to be thought that we're acceding to that application at this stage. It's something I'll think about over the next few days. I'm bound to say that that diary will almost certainly be used, at least in part, in cross-examination of General Smith. So again it's a matter of more immediate concern than simply Mr. Fortin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Josse. And one further question. Have any of these documents been used by General Smith in any written report that has been made available?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The answer is absolutely not. All of the specific documents which I furnished to General Smith or which he requested in connection with the preparation of his expert statement have been disclosed to Defence counsel previously. So they are -- they do not form any basis for any of his expert opinion, which by this point or at this point by virtue of the Chamber's decision is a very narrow area; that is, simply the -- the history, importance, and operation of -- of the Main Staff. So I do not intend to be showing him many documents, if at all, during the course of that expert testimony, because it is, I don't believe, going to be useful necessarily to show him all the other documents that I had discussed with him in connection with the other proposed areas of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, and that's good to know that at least the Fortin diary has to an extent been cleared already. When was the request to the UN as regards the rest of the documents communicated? I'm asking this for one simple reason, so that if we as a Chamber can through our channels accelerate the process, we'll try to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the -- there are 12 documents in total. There was one document that was submitted along with the Fortin diary. That was submitted October 1. And we fully expect all of these documents to be cleared by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With respect to the 11 documents that were kicked out during the course of some recent reviews in connection with General Smith, those were submitted last -- either last week or the end of the week before last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So that disposes of that matter. Yesterday, Mr. Josse, on behalf of the Defence team for General Gvero orally sought an order from the Trial Chamber with a view to barring the Prosecution from questioning the upcoming witness General Rupert Smith on the particular issue raised for the first time by him, that's by General Smith, in his recent proofing session with the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber having heard the submissions of the Defence team for General Gvero and the Prosecution on the matter has considered same and has come to the conclusion that it is not prepared -- cannot grant the order sought. The essence of the Defence complaint is that the disclosure of this information at this late stage is highly prejudicial to the Defence for the reasons outlined in the oral argument yesterday by Mr. Josse. In this instance, the late disclosure arises from the fact that the witness, General Smith, only recently made this statement and had never made it on any previous occasion. It is not a case of non-disclosure by the Prosecution therefore. In these circumstances, we see no basis at law for prohibiting the Prosecution from adducing the evidence from the witness. As to any resulting prejudice, the Defence will have an opportunity to fully cross-examine General Smith. And as his evidence will be given, as I stated earlier, on more than one occasion, they will have adequate time, in our opinion, to prepare for that cross-examination. In addition, if as argued yesterday by Mr. Josse that the Gvero Defence team feels that there is need to recall witnesses on the issue, they can make an ad hoc application to the Trial Chamber in due course and that will receive our due attention. Any other preliminary matters? Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. It may be helpful to throw out the names of the witnesses who we plan to call in lieu of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was coming to that precisely myself. I know that yesterday I invited you -- or the day before yesterday, I think it was, I invited you to sit down together and start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But apart from the list of witnesses now that Dragan Jokic is not testifying, Momir Nikolic is not testifying, we need to also know -- have a revision of the estimated time frame for the rest of the Prosecution case, and this you need to incorporate also within the framework of the other time frame that we spoke about yesterday, namely that necessary for the Rule 98 bis proceedings and decision, and possibly if -- if the Defence case continues -- if the case continues, then for the preparation of the Defence case is particularly what is required by Rule 65 ter. So, yes, in the meantime, perhaps you can update us on who is to come next.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. If we may move into private session for a moment, simply because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, of course. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 16th of October, Mr. Thayer and Mr. McCloskey, you had filed, following an ad hoc request on our part, two scenarios reflecting the rest of your case. One, if the 12th or 16th November break were not to be granted, and the other one, if it were to be granted. We have agreed, as you all know, to grant you that break, which was -- anyway, you know what the reason for that was. I don't need to repeat that. Things have changed now. We will not go back on our decision to grant you the break, because that wouldn't make sense at this point in time. But what we would like to know is now when do you expect the Prosecution case to finish? Because obviously we -- we have one or two witnesses not testifying, and they were not -- they were witnesses that were going to engage us for a considerable length of time. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the calendar and the witnesses, I think we'll give you a more reasonable answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant -- I didn't mean for you to do the exercise now. I would prefer, in fact, to have again something like this, say Monday you will have time to go through the list, but we would appreciate to have that. And we would also appreciate to both of you, both sides, to come back to us with a view to having the oral submissions on the Rule 98 et al. matters as early as possible. We would need to find a slot to give you the opportunity to discuss this in open session and also exchange views with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I have managed to have some discussions already, but -- on that topic, but we'll continue to have discussions. There has been some interest in partially submitting some written material. We're also discussing who goes first, and I will have to look at the law on that. I think Trial Chambers have -- have looked at that differently, but we all -- we will get together on those and inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We just wait. We just wait. Yes. All right. So please come back with an updated estimate of the duration of the rest of your case, and then -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to confuse things or stray into an area that doesn't necessarily concern the Defence, but Your Honour said at line -- at page 56, line 24, that you wanted an answer from the Prosecution now that Dragan Jokic is not testifying. In his response, my learned friend Mr. Thayer, kept and twice referred to fitting Dragan Jokic into the schedule. I'm slightly confused about that. But it maybe the matter remains unresolved. I appreciate that for the most part it's a matter that simply doesn't involve any of the eight parties to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That certainly doesn't involve any of the parties in this case. Yes. Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I simply imagine, Mr. President, that one way or the other Mr. Jokic would be brought back whether it was with everybody present or not, but that we would have to accommodate that at some point. But if that is an entirely in a different courtroom, different time of the day, then we'll take that into account --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- when we're rescheduling our calendar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That is clearer. What he meant is that time will be consumed in dealing with the contempt proceedings, and in his opinion that would have an effect on these proceedings. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Gap-filler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have an hour and 32 minutes before the end of the session, and I do not believe that the Defence will be able to finish today if we start the cross-examination today. Since this is an investigator from the OTP who will not come and testify back on Monday, and we also do not know when he is coming back, and since we are talking about an investigator who will be talking about some documents and he does deal with these documents within his work, I would like to ask you to give us the possibility to cross-examine at another point, at a later stage. I do not put in cause the goodwill of the investigator because I have a great respect for him, but I think that in the course of his work he does have the opportunity to see documents, and he can also see documents that are part of the documents that we wish to use in the cross-examination, so this is why I think that the cross-examination be done in one shot at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've spoken to my colleague about that and told her I would be objecting to that -- to that suggestion. First of all, this witness has been scheduled before many times, Mr. Blaszczyk. They've had the documents for a long time, and so I think they should be ready to start their cross today. I'm -- I'm going to be, I hope, very brief, less than an hour, so there will be time to start their cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I want to make sure that you know what you're saying, because you said about an hour. We have got just 33 minutes for the next break, so that's half an hour. Then there will be the break. You will take another 30 minutes after that, which would leave us with 15 minutes, and you're saying that you expect all cross-examinations to be concluded in 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. And I think that if all goes well, I've cut my direct down, I may be able to finish in around 30 minutes, 40 minutes, in which case there would be enough for somebody to start their cross-examination. The other point I would like to make is that this investigator is a key investigator. We will need to talk with him. And it may be -- it may be that there's a Drina Corps document that I have to talk to him -- that one of us needs to talk to him about, and that's another issue. The Defence estimate is four hours on cross. I cannot -- maybe it will be, but I cannot imagine that it will take that long, and so my preference would be that the cross-examination start, go as far as it can. And I've talked to Mr. Thayer; if necessary, we can go into Monday morning if there is not too much left over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what about Rupert Smith, General Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, then he would perhaps start an hour into Monday morning if necessary. And of course we will -- I will do whatever the Court wishes. That's just my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to start with the witness's testimony, and then we'll come to a decision when you finish with your examination-in-chief. Good morning to you, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We wish to thank you for your patience. I don't want you to think that the Trial Chamber has been playing yo-yo with you, but we've had you on the list. One day you're coming, the next day we're told you're not. You've also earned the nickname of a gap-filler, so I hope we will be able to clear that by your testimony which we are going to start pretty soon. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration with which you are familiar. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Sir, please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Nicholls will see you through his direct. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: My name is Tomasz Blaszczyk. Tomasz Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you are currently employed with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm investigator for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, could you tell us your career in law enforcement up to your employment here with the OTP and when you began your employment with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Back home in Poland I was Polish officer. I began my work with the police in 1981 as uniformed police officers -- officer, and after graduated police academy in 1986, I became an instructor. And I used to work as instructor until 1989, and since 1989 I used to work in criminal department in my region, region of Dojsk [phoen]. At the beginning I used to work in rapid reaction team and I moved to investigation and operation section. In 1998, 1999, I moved to drug investigation unit, and then to another unit, central investigation bureau which emerged from drug investigation unit and crime investigation unit. During my work with the police I was deployed three times to Bosnia as international police task officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During any of that -- that prior law enforcement experience in Poland, did you ever have to testify?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just very briefly, when were you working in Bosnia? Can you just tell us which dates you worked in Bosnia and what you were doing, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: First time I was shortly in Bosnia it was 1992. At that time mostly I was deployed to former Krajina or so-called Krajina in Croatia, and about two, three weeks in Bosnia, and three times I was deployed in Bosnia. First time in 1996, then 1998 and 2001, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was with IPTF those last times?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. These three times I was deployed as IPTF officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again very briefly, what was the purpose or what were your duties with the IPTF?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: The IPTF was a part of United Nations mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The IPTF was involved in training, certificating, monitoring the activity of the local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you begin working with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I started to work with OTP it was January 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And briefly which -- which investigations have been your focus of your work here?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Most of the times, almost since the beginning I have been attached to Srebrenica investigation, and except few months in 2000 -- at the end of 2005 when I was deployed temporarily to Haradinaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you now some questions about this big collection of documents which is referred to as the Drina Corps collection. First of all, are you familiar -- you don't need to explain the whole process now, but are you familiar with the process by which the OTP came into possession of this collection?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall just roughly the ERN range of the Drina Corps collection?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is -- the ERN range for this collection started from 0425 onwards, about 350.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you personally first hear that this document collection was in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but it was sometime in the middle of December 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where was the Drina Corps collection of documents located when you first heard that it was in our possession?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: First time when I heard that, about this Drina collection, is when the Drina collection was located already in IP -- sorry, ICTY office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's our field office there?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Field office, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how did you learn -- what were your sources of, how did you learn about how this large collection of documents came into our possession in the field office in Banja Luka in December 2004?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: First I learn it from my management, this mean from my team leader and the people who were working together with me and then from the investigator on the field, investigator from the field office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what's the name of that investigator who you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Finn Tollefsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, briefly we'll go over some documents in a minute, but can you briefly tell the Court how this collection of documents we call the Drina Corps collection came to be delivered to the Banja Luka field office?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Authority of Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina, received information that this collection is located in military barracks in Serbia and Montenegro, in the place called Gornji Mlanovac, military barracks of the army of Serbia and Montenegro. And the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska together with Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska conducted action, joint action on the territory of Serbia and Montenegro to collect and transfer these documents to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you know, from whom did the OTP learn that this archive had been brought to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. The first time OTP received this information from the liaison officer for the relation with ICTY Trifun Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak slower, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You got the message. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Gornja Milanovac, you said, is where the -- where the collection was located in the military barracks in Serbia. Can you tell us -- I don't have a map. Can you tell us where that is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. The place is located about 100 kilometres south of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how close is it to Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: About -- I guess about 200 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you remember, do you remember the date in December when we learned about this collection from Mr. Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. It was 9 of December, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you a series of documents and ask you just a few questions about them. The first is 02810. It should appear on the screen in front of you, and I have hard copies here if you need to look at those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's no objection, may I give the witness a list of the exhibits I plan to use with him? They're the same ones that are on our list that was distributed a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this first document - excuse me - is Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence decision dated 8 December 2004. Briefly can you tell us what this document is, what it's about?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. This is decision signed by Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, Milovan Stankovic decision about appointing the commission for taking over, sealing and handing over the archive material from the army of Republika Srpska located in Serbia and Montenegro. And also in this document we have the names of the people who were appointed as a commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think the document is fairly self-explanatory. I'll go to the next one. 02811. It's on the screen now. This is from, again, the 8th of December, 2004, and this one from the General Staff of the VRS. Can you -- same question for each of these. Can you tell us what this document is and what it is about?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. This is more or less the same document, the same contents of the document but signed by the -- the head of General Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, General Major Novak Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the next document, 02812, again referring to the process of retrieving this collection of documents. Again we're speaking of the 8th of December, 2004. This will be another Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence document. Decision, rather. Can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a decision of the approval of the official trip for -- for the member of the commission, actually for the head of the commission Mirko Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next one, 02813. This is an 8 December 2004 record on the receiving of the archival material and archival artefacts, another General Staff document. Now it's on the screen. Can you tell us about this document, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Also this is the record prepared by the head of the commission Colonel Mirko Matic. The document was prepared on the 8th of December, 2004, but was signed on 9 December 2004 by Mirko Matic, the two other members of the commission, Dragan Radisic, Miljan Sisic, and also by the member of the army of Serbia and Montenegro, Dragan Brcan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we are can see here that the amount of -- well, the commission received 16 wooden cases of material. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah, this is right. Actually, there were 16 boxes using for explosive and ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 02806, please. This is the 10th of January, 2005, report from the Ministry of the Interior. It should be on the screen in a minute. This is a longer document with more detail, but can you just tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. This is letter supplied by the Republika Srpska ministry of interior related to the provision of the [Indiscernible] Drina Corps archive. The letter provide a summary of the events leading to the Ministry of Interior taking possession of the Drina Corps archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And does it also address how those documents came to be delivered to the OTP field office?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. That is information also how the document -- how the collection was delivered to -- to the OTP office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next one, 02805, please, a very similar document in content. 20th of December, 2004, from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I say, Your Honour, part of this document was redacted because part of it had absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with this topic. That was disclosed to the Defence in an unredacted form, I think. I'm not sure how that happened, but they've had it. But for this purposes and in public I'm using the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: It's more or less the same contents as the previous document. It's also consists information about circumstances of obtaining the Drina Corps archive from the territory of Serbia and Montenegro and also information how this archive ended up in OTP office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And very briefly, the six documents we've just reviewed, how did we come into possession of these documents, reports, decisions, orders about the seizure and delivery of the Drina Corps collection of documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: The two last documents we received from our request from the authority of Ministry of Interior, from the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. The first four documents, they are documents received from the witness who had been testified by OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to switch now and ask you a couple questions about your -- your personal involvement with processing the collection. After first being told by management about the collection and speaking to Finn Tollefsen from Banja Luka field office, where did you go? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I was ordered to go to Zagreb field office where the archive supposed to arrived and make the initial assessment of this archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it was 17 of December, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do, briefly, if you can describe what -- what the process was of handling this large number of documents when they arrived in our Zagreb field office.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I remember that the archive arrived to the Zagreb field office, ICTY field office, the same day when I was there. I was already there, actually. And it came with UN truck with the escort, with UN security officer, and it came with 23 cardboard boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- now, so these -- we saw on the receipt there were 16 boxes delivered to the field office, and now you've said 23 boxes. Can you explain that, why there's a different number of boxes arriving at Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. The first to the ICTY field office in Banja Luka there were delivered 16 boxes, military boxes used for ammunition, explosive materials, weapons, full of the documents, and in Banja Luka -- in the Banja Luka field office the boxes were repacked to 23 cardboard boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me show you number 02808, and the one after that will be 02809, two photographs. They're not particularly interesting, but this is a photograph of a big box. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah, this is photograph of one the box -- one of the box used to keeping the archive material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And this is one of the boxes that was received -- that they were originally received in from the authorities in Republika Srpska, or is this one of the 23 boxes?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No, this is one of the box which we received from the authority of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka field office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness should first answer the question that is did he ever see the original boxes in which the documents arrived. I'm not sure the witness was able to see the original boxes sent by the authorities of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That question is two lines down but I can ask it now. Did you take this photo? Did you see these boxes?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No. Personally, I never seen these boxes but I seen the photos taken by our field office investigator in the Banja Luka field office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could have 02809 on the screen. Tell us what's in this photo when it comes up.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: This is another photo taken by investigator on the field office in Banja Luka, Finn Tollefsen, and this depict also one of the box and full of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were the boxes -- just to be very clear because we'll get to the receipts in a minute, but when the box -- when this material, all these documents, came to be transported from the Zagreb field office here to The Hague, did they come in the same 23 boxes or were they repacked again?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No. The boxes were again repacked into 55 and other smaller boxes and then sent to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very briefly, what's the -- what was the point of repacking these from 16 boxes to 23 to 55? Why was that done?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: It was done for easier handling of this material because it was weighed sometimes even more than 100 kilogrammes. It was very difficult to handle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you very, very briefly tell us about the process of how the boxes arrived here in The Hague, how they came to be here?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When they arrived. Excuse me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. The boxes were sent from the Zagreb field office on the 3rd of January 2005, and arrived here in The Hague on the 4th of January, 2005, and all the boxes were stored in evidence unit in the vault.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then we won't go through that but then is that when the process of assigning ERN numbers and scanning and all the normal processes associated with evidence takes place?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. After they arrive here and are put in the evidence vault, without going into all the details, is that when these documents are processed the way other evidence is, assigned ERN numbers, scanned into the system and so forth?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. The organising process of these documents started on the 16 -- as far as I remember on the 13 January 2005, and first each document -- okay. It took some time, of course, but it lasted about few months, and each document received its own ERN number, was scanned and put in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we look at some receipts now and some records. These are all together in 02807, and this is my last exhibit. Thank you. Now, there's several pages to this, and I'd like to just -- just very briefly go through page by page and tell us what this chain of receipts and records shows.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Okay. The -- the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we have up here 04247825, for the record, it's the first page.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: The first page this is declaration on receipt of materials signed by OTP investigator on the field, Finn Tollefsen, and by Dragan Milosevic, the person who handed over the archive to our field office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, it says at the bottom in the handwritten portion by investigator Finn Toleffsen, 24 cardboard boxes and you earlier, I believe, said 23 cardboard boxes came to Zagreb. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It happened because the second day when the boxes arrived to the Banja Luka field office and the investigator Toleffsen received also another boxes, two boxes contained the tapes seized in other operation by the MUP of Republika Srpska, but the tapes had nothing to do with archive. And he counted -- counted also this -- this box.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could we go to the next page. 04247826 is the ERN number. What does this statement of enclosure tell us?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a statement of enclosure signed by the head of the office in Zagreb confirming that the boxes, this material, arrived in Zagreb on the 17 December 2004, at 1630 hundred hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it also discusses that they are repacked.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. Also there is information that these boxes were repacked into 57 boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please, which is 04247827, a list of box numbers. What does this tell us? The date is the 20th of December, 2004.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: This is information how the boxes which arrived to the Zagreb field office were repacked into 55 boxes in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And now can we go to the next page of this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. At the end is handwritten note that mention the 55 boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, earlier we saw -- a minute ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Does that mean that the extra box, what he explained would be number 24, was then repacked in two boxes, making a total of 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's where I was going, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, please, Your Honour. That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you explain, you earlier discussed the number 57; this receipt is 55. Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, because the two additional boxes they consist of the tapes received also from the Banja Luka field office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We're almost -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I've lost track of when the next break is. I've only got a very little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next break is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'm really nearly done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it will help you get back on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're 25 minutes break, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go now to the next page, which is ERN 04247829. It's page 5 of this document. And this is a UN ICTY cargo manifest. It will come up in a moment, and you can just tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Okay. This UN ICTY cargo manifest signed by head of the office in Zagreb field office, and also by the person named Dirk Bruks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it says here mode of transportation, truck, Europe. It's pretty self-explanatory, but what is this document for?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: This is for -- for the trip, you know, used by the truck driver, the trip team which drove to -- to The Hague from Zagreb field office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And here we see that are 1 to 57 boxes of evidence. Without saying what it is, the area here that's been redacted, did it have anything to do with the Drina Corps collection, that other material that was transported in this truck?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No. The redacted things, you know, are nothing to do with the archive material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Last page, page 6, which is 04247830. It's a packing list with some signatures at the bottom, and it shows that there are 55 boxes of documents and that boxes 56 and 57 are evidence tapes. Can you just tell us about this document very briefly?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. This is packing list prepared by Thomas Osorio, the head of the UN ICTY office in Zagreb, and the final recipient signature on this document is the member of evidence unit from ICTY. This mean that these 55 boxes and two another boxes consisted of tapes from Banja Luka were received by member of evidence unit here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was, we can see 4th of January, 2005; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah. The transport was sent on the 3rd of January, 2005 and arrived to The Hague on the 4th of January, 2005 and was received by member of the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Mr. McCloskey. No, no, no. It's -- it's directed to Mr. McCloskey. You have no problem with your extension number being communicated to the whole world, do you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's all right. I'll -- if I get any calls I'll change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hadn't noticed, thought of that. That concludes my direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We now have approximately three-quarters of an hour. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you'll finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to clear up a few matters at the beginning. You have been shown a document that I would like to see again, 2807, Prosecutor's Exhibit 2807. It is dated 13 December 2004, and I see it was signed by a man named Dragi Milosevic. There are two more signatures there. But do you agree that your signature isn't there?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You agree that you were not present when this document was drafted? Yes, meaning you were present or not present?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From this document I see that then, on the 13 December 2004, 16 boxes were turned over. That is, on the 15th and 16th that they were repacked into 24 boxes in Banja Luka. You were not present during the repackaging of this material from 16 into 24 boxes, were you?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you were not present.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now see the next page of this document. On the next page, towards the bottom of this document we see that the liaison officer received 24 boxes from the OTP office in Banja Luka, and they were repacked again into 27 boxes this time to facilitate transport. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fifty-seven boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Fifty-seven. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, you were not present when this was done?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I was present at that time, at this stage. I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you took part in the repackaging of those 24 into 57 boxes?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, that was on the 17th December 2004, at least that's what we read here. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 17 of December. Actually we started on the 17 of December but it lasted about two days, I think, until the 19 of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did you inventory the documentation contained in the boxes?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had no time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone else had who had time to do it?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No. There were present only me, head of the office, and one of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me what was done with those boxes on the 19th December when the repacking was finished?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: You mean these new boxes, the 55 boxes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: They were kept at the field office in -- in Zagreb until 3rd [Realtime transcript read in error "5th"] of January, 2005, where they were sent to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say the date again, because it's not in the record -- oh, yes, it is. Sorry. It's all right. In the meantime it was corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I think there's an error in the transcript on line 21, page 79. I believe the witness said 3rd of January and we've got 5th. I heard 3rd, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It was kept in the field office until 3rd of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3rd of January. And that corresponds with the date you see at the bottom of the document right to the left of the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that, among other things, there existed tapes in one of those boxes. Did you listen to them?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody else listen to them in your presence?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No. No. For sure not in the field office in Zagreb, but for sure here in -- in-house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say in-house, you mean here in The Hague, or you mean the field office in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I mean here in The Hague, in our building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- you explained to us here the tapes were separated because they were not related to the Drina Corps. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I received this information from the investigator from the field. I later on also I learn it from the information we received from the authority of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that investigator tell you that he had listened to those tapes?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to this first document, those tapes were among the other material of the Drina Corps that had been turned over on the 13th of April. Do you agree with that? Sorry, 13 December.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: As far as I know, the tapes were handed over to our field office in Banja Luka on the 14th of December. No, I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you cannot confirm that they were listened to?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness answered before he heard the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need the answer which we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is you cannot confirm that the tapes had been listened to in the meantime. [Previous translation continues] ... It was not in transcript, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still we have that too. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, you were present when all this documentation arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I am not sure that I was present when the documentation arrived to The Hague, but I was present when the documentation arrived to the Zagreb field office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when -- whether and when -- something was misinterpreted here, that it arrived in Greater Serbia. I meant Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know they have a databank. That will be corrected in due course. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, and if yes, when the documentation received from Zagreb was inventoried, those 23 boxes and the additional one? Was it inventoried here in the OTP in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it was done during the quite long process in the evidence unit vault by the team assigned to do this task. The documentation was organised into categories and then MFI'd, given ERN, scanned and put into the system. It lasted quite a long time. If you mean inventory in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from the authorities of Republika Srpska ever attend the process of inventorying this documentation?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I'm not aware about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] The answer is I'm not aware about it?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't know. I think rather not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know if somebody from the Yugoslav authorities was present because that documentation had been taken from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I think not, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit 2809, the picture that we have been shown. Were you present when these boxes were opened upon arrival in The Hague and when these documents were taken out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw. The question was different than what I expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So do you wish to hear the question again or are you in a position to answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't present when that picture was taken here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But if I can just be clear. This picture and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- was -- is from Banja Luka was the testimony on direct not in The Hague which is what my friend said. I don't know if that was a correct translation or what the error is here, but this picture is from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Then I must have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, were you present when the documents were taken out from the boxes shown in the picture.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Not from these boxes, not from these military boxes. The boxes were handed over first to Banja Luka field office and the documentation from the boxes were packed into cardboard boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, if we look at these documents here, were these documents taken out of one particular box or is it just documentation that was randomly photographed standing next to a box?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I cannot say that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek or who would like to go next?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can handle it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is John Ostojic as you know we've met before. I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara. I'm going to ask you some questions here today to clarify some matters. Sir, am I correct that -- and I know you shared with us the -- essentially the chain of custody with respect to the documents once the OTP was in possession of them from December '04 through today's date, correct? That's the essence of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well as an investigator working for the OTP on the Srebrenica case, could you share with us what the chain of custody of these documents were for the nine years prior to the OTP getting into possession of them?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Base of -- on the information I have, you know, base of on the statements we collected from few witnesses, I know that this documentation was first collected by the Drina Corps common -- command in January, between January and April in 1996, and were kept in Drina Corps command and then were sent to Bijeljina for some time. In 1997 came back to Sokolac to the 5th Corps command and, as far as I know, was sent to Zvornik and Mali Zvornik in spring 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, share with me if you will, sir, why you think it's important to maintain a proper chain of custody for documents that may be used as evidence in a criminal proceeding. I want to hear from you think why it may or may not be important?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Of course this is important, because we can show -- we can see if anybody interfere into these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier today upon my learned friend's questioning that you went to Zagreb on the 17th of December '04 in order to make an assessment of the documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Initial assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't hear the word "initial" earlier but I'll accept that. What did you do to make an initial assessment. Tell me what your process is, if you will?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: When I arrive to Zagreb actually nobody knows at that time which kind of collection it is. We're not sure that this is Drina Corps collection or Main Staff collection. I would like to check. Actually I was sent by my supervisor to Zagreb to check what kind of documents they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So am I correct then the conversation you had with Finn Tollefsen, you didn't discuss with him what the contents of these boxes were?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact conversation, but I don't think that Finn was aware what -- what is the contents of these documents, fully aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because when my learned friend asked you how did you come to learn that the documents were in Banja Luka, you mentioned your management whose name you didn't give us and that would be okay and then you also mentioned the investigator in the field and you mentioned Finn Tollefsen. So you didn't talk to him about whether he opened the boxes or determined whether the collection would be relevant specifically for the unit that you were working which would have been Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I talked to him to the phone but I don't remember the exact conversation but it wasn't clear, you know, during this conversation this is the collection of the Drina Corps, the Main Staff or any other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to your first meeting when you went to Zagreb on the 17th of December, 04. Did you maintain a diary or keep notes which, typically, I suggest an investigator should do in making an assessment or initial assessment of what you were doing, namely identifying or examining documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Maybe not notes, but I made some kind of copies of a few documents relevant to July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now you had a copy machine available to you?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask you to observe a short pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are perfectly right. You're both speaking in English, so please allow a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, now were your reports back to the Office of the Prosecution all oral or did you have to maintain like an information report or something to document what exactly it is that you did? Did you photocopy documents? Did you review documents or any of that sort?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: As I told you, I made some photocopies of these documents from this collection but I had no time even to prepare only inventory list or something like that. There were too many documents, too many pages, 350.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right and forgive me because I may have misspoke. I'm not asking you if you inventoried each page on the visit of the 17th of December, 2004. I'm saying as a reasonably prudent investigator, wouldn't you or did you, sir, keep notes of what you actually did to suggest as follows: I arrived in Zagreb at this time. I was given X amount of boxes of documents. I opened the documents. I found that they may or may not be relevant to the Srebrenica case to which I had been assigned since January 2003, although nobody knew that until I came to visit the offices in Zagreb. And then just to tell them what you did basically, how you then kept the documents from being accessible to others, if you will. You're telling me you made no such written report at that time or any time thereafter to any of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: No, I didn't make any specific report regarding this collection. I just informed my supervisor through the phone and when I came back to -- to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's not as important to me once the Prosecution received the documents, as you can imagine, in 2004, and we're not claiming that the Prosecutor in any -- at any time manipulated or tried to distort or alter those documents, but let's go back to the nine and a half year gap from the time the documents were essentially created and from -- up to the time the OTP was in possession of those documents. Are you aware, sir, that after 1998 who was actually the -- personally responsible to maintain and keep those documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I am not aware who was personally responsible for these documents, but I know where the documents were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the name Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were on this team now for four plus years. Are you aware of the fact that Dragan Obrenovic was personally supervised and was in charge of the documents, keeping them supposedly in a safe place?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: It was mention in one of the statement handed over to OTP by the authorities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for how long? Tell the Court how long Dragan Obrenovic had the only keys, right, and had the only access to this Banja Luka collection of documents. For how long did he have that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't know how long Dragan Obrenovic had the keys from this -- from -- from this building or collections, but even I don't know whether Dragan Obrenovic had a key, you know, from this collections, but I know that it was mentioned in one of the statement, statement of Nebojsa Vukicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. What if anything as a reasonably prudent investigator did you do, sir, to verify whether Nebojsa Vukicevic was correct or not in stating that Dragan Obrenovic had the only keys to the storage area where the Drina Corps collection was maintained from 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I didn't speak with Dragan -- sorry, with Nebojsa Vukicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: About this collection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you have an opportunity at that time, sir, to discuss with him the fact that he had at all times maintained the keys, the only keys, I suggest, and was the only person who had access to those documents? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I know the story of Dragan Obrenovic. He told us how he was involved in this archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what did he say? Did he -- it's true that he personally supervised the documents once they came to Zvornik and that he was the only person who had the keys to the storage where those documents were kept? Did you inquire about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: As far as I -- I remember and I recall, and Dragan Obrenovic facilitate, you know, this passing the border by this archive to Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever speak to Nebojsa Vukicevic about the fact that he states and I'll quote it for you because I don't know if you remember but you may, that: "Dragan Obrenovic was responsible for the storage of it," being the documents, "in the above-mentioned place from April 1998 through March of 1999." Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I never spoke with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Why I should spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, to find out if at any point he either created documents, to find out if he ever added things to documents, to find out and to ensure us that the documents that are in your possession are actually authentic and, therefore, reliable. You don't think that would be important?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yeah, it is important, but I know that my colleagues from other team, they were involved to find out who learned to get evidence, how this collection came to our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me with this. In the hierarchy of investigators, where would you fall with respect to the Srebrenica case currently? Are you the lead investigator, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: We can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you become the lead investigator?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: When the previous lead investigator left the Tribunal one year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One year ago?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: One and a half year ago, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Bruce Bursik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with Mr. Bursik whether or not any of the investigators at any time followed up to determine how was it that Dragan Obrenovic, an accused, a person who admitted his guilt, was convicted and sentenced, how was it that he had maintained crucial documents, I suggest, for a period of approximately one year and no one had either asked him that or followed up with Mr. Nebojsa Vukicevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean, it's a compound, confusing, very long question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's confusing at all, and I don't know if that's a basis for an objection, but if the witness can't understand the question, I'll be more than happy to restate it but we don't need the Prosecution to assist the witness at this point, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not assisting I'm objecting to an improper compound question which has three or four different elements in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's split it or you rephrase it, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You know, compound questions, Your Honour, on cross-examination are permitted if you're, in essence, putting your case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- so it is an improper objection but in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you answer it for me?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I never discuss it with Mr. Bruce Bursik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think it's important to find out from wither Dragan Obrenovic or Mr. Vukicevic whether or not there was any alterations or modifications or changes with respect to these documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I think it is important and was discussed with Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
